sentence: If you follow aviation history, December 17, 1903 is one of those dates that really matters.
That morning near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville and Wilbur Wright got their Flyer off the ground for the first successful powered flight by a heavier-than-air machine.
The first hop was only 12 seconds and 120 feet, which sounds tiny now, but it changed everything.
People had flown in balloons before, and plenty of inventors had experimented with gliders, but the Wright brothers combined power, control, and sustained flight in one aircraft.
Their key breakthrough wasn’t just getting into the air — it was being able to steer and manage the plane once it was there.
So yes, a short flight on a cold beach is absolutely worth a post today.
I still catch myself saying “the dark side of the Moon,” but it’s kind of a misleading phrase.
The far side isn’t always dark — it gets sunlight just like the side we see, just at different times.
What people usually mean is the “far side,” because that side mostly faces away from Earth.
We keep seeing nearly the same lunar face because the Moon rotates once in about the same time it takes to orbit Earth.
It’s like it’s slowly turning while going around us, keeping one side pointed our way.
So the Moon isn’t hiding some permanently dark half; it’s just tidally locked, which is a cooler and more accurate way to say it.
Ever walked out into bright sun and suddenly sneezed like your nose hit a secret button?
Turns out that’s a real thing called the photic sneeze reflex, and it happens to a surprising number of people.
It’s not an allergy to sunlight, and the light isn’t irritating your nose the way pollen or dust would.
The basic idea is that in some people, the nerve signals for bright light and sneezing seem to get a little crossed.
It also tends to run in families, so if you do it, there’s a decent chance someone else in your family does too.
Honestly, it’s kind of funny that stepping outside can make your face reboot for a second.
I used to think deleting a file meant it was instantly wiped off the drive forever.
Most of the time, deletion just removes the “map” that tells your computer where that file lives, so the space is marked as available.
The actual bits can sit there for a while until something new gets saved over them.
That’s why recovery tools can sometimes bring deleted files back, especially if you stop using the drive right away.
It’s also why selling or tossing an old computer without properly wiping the drive can be risky.
If you really want something gone, use a secure erase option or encrypt the drive before getting rid of it.
I saw someone say “our currency is up 10%, so everyone is 10% richer now,” and it’s not really that simple.
An exchange rate just tells you how much one currency trades for against another, not what your paycheck can buy at home.
If rent, groceries, fuel, and bills are still expensive, a stronger currency doesn’t magically make daily life easier.
It can help with imported goods or overseas travel, sure, but that benefit isn’t spread evenly to everyone.
Living standards depend on wages, prices, jobs, debt, public services, and a bunch of other things people actually deal with day to day.
So yes, a currency can “strengthen” on the news, while ordinary people still feel like nothing has changed at the checkout line.
Tiny geography note because I used to mix this up too: Holland and the Netherlands aren’t exactly the same thing.
The Netherlands is the whole country, while Holland is just one part of it.
To be extra specific, there are two provinces called North Holland and South Holland, and they include places like Amsterdam, Rotterdam, and The Hague.
Since those areas are so well known, people often say “Holland” when they mean the entire Netherlands.
It’s kind of like saying “England” when you really mean the whole UK — common, but not quite accurate.
So if someone says Holland, you’ll usually know what they mean, but “the Netherlands” is the safer name for the country.
People sometimes talk about “Indian food” like it’s one big thing, but that misses so much of what makes it amazing.
In Kerala, you’ll find coconut, curry leaves, and seafood showing up in ways that feel totally different from the buttery gravies and tandoori dishes people often associate with Punjab.
Go to Gujarat and you might get a sweet-salty dal or fluffy dhokla, while in Bengal mustard oil and fish are a whole love language.
Even the breads change from place to place: rotis, dosas, appams, parathas, puris, and so many more.
Climate, crops, religion, trade, and family traditions all shape what ends up on the plate.
So when we say we love Indian food, it’s worth remembering we’re really talking about dozens of regional food worlds, each with its own story.
One thing I love about Hebrew is how many words seem to grow out of a little cluster of consonants, usually three of them.
For example, a root can show up in verbs, nouns, and adjectives that all circle the same basic idea, like a word family with a shared DNA.
It’s a really helpful way to notice connections, especially when you’re learning new vocabulary and suddenly a word feels less random.
That said, it’s not a magic code that explains every single word perfectly.
Languages are messy, old, borrowed-from-everywhere things, so some words have shifted meanings or don’t fit the pattern neatly.
Still, once you start seeing the roots, Hebrew can feel a little less like a list to memorize and more like a web of related ideas.
Jazz improvisation isn’t just somebody throwing random notes into the air and hoping they land.
Most players are listening to the chords, feeling the groove, and choosing notes that make sense in that moment.
It’s kind of like having a conversation: you can say something new, but you’re still using a shared language.
The rhythm, the style of the tune, and even little musical phrases everyone knows help guide what happens next.
That’s why a solo can feel spontaneous and surprising, but still fit perfectly with the band.
To me, the magic is that jazz musicians can be free without being totally untethered.
I always heard that sugar turns kids into tiny tornadoes, but the research on that is a lot less clear than the legend.
In studies where parents and kids don’t know who actually got sugar, sugar usually doesn’t cause a noticeable jump in hyperactivity.
What often does make kids wild is the setting: birthday parties, holidays, sleepovers, excitement, noise, and staying up late.
There’s even evidence that if parents think their child had sugar, they may watch for “hyper” behavior more closely and notice it more.
That doesn’t mean candy is suddenly a health food, of course, just that blaming every zoomie session on sugar is probably too simple.
Kids can absolutely get wound up after dessert, but the science says the dessert may not be the main reason.
